content: The evidence supporting the use of psychotherapy and medication for Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) is limited. Some individuals may choose to avoid these treatments or may not derive sufficient benefit from them. It has been suggested that diagnostic categorization may have limited utility in guiding therapeutic interventions for BPD. In some cases, understanding borderline behaviors as partially adaptive requires examining an individual’s past and current relationships. This perspective can help identify the most effective ways to support individuals with BPD. Psychological services that are group-based often encourage clients to engage in socialization and participate in both solitary and group activities. These services may be offered in settings such as day centers. Therapeutic communities, particularly in Europe, have historically been an example of such services, although their use has declined. Many of these communities have specialized in treating severe personality disorders. Psychiatric rehabilitation services aim to assist individuals with mental health challenges, including BPD, by reducing psychosocial disability, promoting engagement in meaningful activities, and mitigating stigma and social exclusion. Mutual-support or co-counseling groups, often run by and for individuals with BPD, are also available. The goal of these groups may be to achieve full recovery rather than continued reliance on mental health services. Data suggests that a significant proportion of individuals diagnosed with BPD can achieve remission within one to two years. A longitudinal study found that six years after diagnosis, 56% of individuals with BPD demonstrated good psychosocial functioning, compared to only 26% at baseline. However, vocational achievement among individuals with BPD was more limited compared to those with other personality disorders. Those whose symptoms had remitted were more likely to have positive relationships with a spouse or partner, at least one parent, good work or school performance, a sustained work or school history, good global functioning, and overall good psychosocial functioning. In clinical practice, psychotherapy and medication are often combined, but there is limited data on the effectiveness of this approach. Efficacy studies frequently evaluate interventions when added to treatment as usual (TAU), which may include general psychiatric services, supportive counseling, medication, and psychotherapy. One small study, which excluded individuals with comorbid Axis I disorders, found that outpatients undergoing Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) and taking the antipsychotic olanzapine showed significantly greater improvement on some BPD-related measures compared to those undergoing DBT and taking a placebo. However, the olanzapine group also experienced weight gain and elevated cholesterol levels. Another small study found that patients who underwent DBT and then took fluoxetine (Prozac) showed no significant improvements, whereas those who underwent DBT and then took a placebo did show significant improvements. The treatment of BPD presents unique challenges. For example, individuals with BPD may harm themselves or withdraw from treatment if they perceive rejection or invalidation, even in hospital care settings. Clinicians may emotionally distance themselves from individuals with BPD as a form of self-protection or due to the stigma associated with the diagnosis. This can create a self-fulfilling prophecy and perpetuate a cycle of stigmatization, to which both the patient and therapist may contribute. Some psychotherapies, such as DBT, were specifically developed to address issues related to interpersonal sensitivity and maintaining a therapeutic relationship. Adherence to medication regimens is also a significant challenge, partly due to adverse effects. Dropout rates in medication trials range from 50% to 88%. Comorbid disorders, particularly substance use disorders, can further complicate efforts to achieve remission. Psychotherapies and medications are part of the broader context of mental health services and psychosocial needs related to BPD. However, the evidence base for both remains limited. Some individuals may choose to forgo these treatments or may not benefit sufficiently from them. It has been argued that diagnostic categorization alone may not be sufficient to guide therapeutic work in this area. In some cases, understanding borderline behaviors as partially adaptive requires considering an individual’s past and current relationships. This approach can help identify strategies to enhance self-efficacy, establish social roles, and foster a sense of being valued by others, ultimately boosting self-esteem.
